features.heroLead: Filmtone starts from a preset, lets you judge color, light, and shadow in playback or before/after, and keeps deeper LUT controls available when the simple path is not enough. This page separates the Web trial path, the iPhone save/share path, and the Mac playback/export path.

features.cardsTitle: Start from a preset, then adjust only what you need.
features.card1Body: Pause, scrub, compare before/after, or keep playback running. The workflow is built so video decisions are not made from stills only.
features.card2Title: Use preview and proxies to reduce waiting
features.card2Body: For heavier footage, preview and proxy paths keep the edit moving while still treating camera-original media as the source.
features.card3Body: Adjust streaks from bright points while previewing the result. Threshold, chromatic separation, and length stay visible while you decide.
features.card4Title: Use the same color direction for stills
features.card4Body: After finishing a video, covers and thumbnails can follow the same color direction.

features.workflowBullet1: Use stills for covers, thumbnails, gallery frames and supporting images around the clip.
features.workflowBullet2: Keep color direction consistent instead of rebuilding it in a separate photo-first workflow.

controls.bloomToggleHint: Soft glow that spreads from bright areas (bloom).
controls.bloomThresholdHint: Only pixels brighter than this level contribute strongly to the glow.
controls.halationToggleHint: Colored glow around very bright edges (halation).
controls.finishToolsMistOutcome: Soften the whole image with a finished haze.
controls.finishToolsCrossOutcome: Turn point lights into a visible optical signature.
controls.finishToolsTextureOutcome: Add grain and falloff to make the image feel finished.
controls.finishToolsLensOutcome: Add subtle fringing and softness to break the digital clean edge.
controls.finishToolsMotionOutcome: Shape motion smear and trails while you judge in playback.
controls.artifactsSectionHint: Grain, vignette, glow, halation, and related film-look controls.
controls.sourceTrimSectionHint: Adjust the imported image before the film look—exposure, color, highlights, and shadows.
controls.compressionHint: Softens bright tones with a film-style shoulder curve. Not file or data compression.
controls.compressionRangeHint: Widens or narrows how much of the tonal range that softness affects (highlights through shadows).
controls.printContrastHint: Adds contrast in the print-style stage—separate from the main Contrast slider in the grading stack.
controls.rgbShiftToggleHint: Turn chromatic aberration on or off. It can break the image if pushed too far, so use it only when needed.
controls.grainRadialMixHint: Near 0: even grain. Near 1: stronger toward frame edges (not chromatic aberration). At 1 matches the previous default.
controls.lightShaftsToggleHint: Volumetric beams of light radiating from a point in the frame.
controls.shaftIntensityHint: Overall brightness of the light shafts. Zero means off.
controls.shaftDecayHint: How quickly the beams fade as they spread from the source.
controls.shaftOriginXHint: Horizontal position of the light source (0 = left, 1 = right).
controls.shaftOriginYHint: Vertical position of the light source (0 = top, 1 = bottom).
controls.crossFilterToggleHint: Star-shaped light streaks from bright points, like a physical cross-screen lens filter.
controls.crossFilterSpikesHint: Number of light spikes: 4-point (classic cross), 6-point (snow cross), or 8-point (sunny cross).
controls.crossFilterAngleHint: Rotates the spike pattern. 0° places the first spike pointing right.
controls.crossFilterLengthHint: How far the light spikes extend from bright sources.
controls.crossFilterThresholdHint: Only pixels brighter than this level produce spikes. Higher values limit the effect to the brightest points.
controls.crossFilterChromaticHint: Color dispersion along each spike, like light diffracting through a ruled grating.
controls.crossFilterSizeLimitHint: Suppresses streaks from large light sources. Higher values limit the effect to small point sources, excluding lamps, sun, or other area lights.
controls.crossFilterRandomnessHint: Controls what fraction of light sources produce streaks. Lower values create a sparse, selective effect.
controls.crossFilterHardModeOverrideHint: Hard Mode forces these values internally. Switch to Soft to control them manually.
controls.crossFilterMinSpacingHint: Reduces the intensity of nearby overlapping streaks while preserving the light cluster shape. Use this to declutter dense groups such as chandeliers.
controls.dustAmountHint: Adds random dust particles over the image, like aged film stock.
controls.scratchAmountHint: Adds vertical film scratches that drift across the frame.
controls.shutterAngleHint: 180° is the normal-source baseline with no added blur; above 180° adds a slow-shutter extension.
controls.trailIntensityHint: Extends afterimages beyond the shutter window; it only affects active slow-shutter motion.

batch.tipWebglAccurate: When on, seeks each frame and grades via readPixels — very slow but closest to Edit. Off (default) uses fast ffmpeg one-pass (approximate). .cube LUT preferred; Params approximated in ffmpeg.

roadmap.title: Roadmap — Filmtone
roadmap.description: Filmtone development roadmap — upcoming features and planned improvements for Desktop and Web.
roadmap.heroBody: Our development priorities, shaped by real creative workflows. Features move from idea to release as they prove their value.

batchJpegPng.title: Batch JPEG / PNG grading
batchJpegPng.description: Grade entire folders at once — apply your chosen preset to every image in a directory.

singleVideoExport.title: Single video export
singleVideoExport.description: Apply the same look to one short MP4 and export with your grade baked in.

fourPresets.title: 4 film-inspired presets
fourPresets.description: Kodak Portra 400, Fuji Pro 400H, Kodak Ektar 100, and Ilford HP5 Plus.

browserDemo.title: Browser demo
browserDemo.description: Try presets on your own photos before downloading the desktop app.

shareLook.title: Share your look via URL
shareLook.description: Generate a link that opens the browser demo with your exact preset settings.

desktopExportWorkflow033.title: Desktop v0.3 — export & preview refinement
desktopExportWorkflow033.description: Clearer switching between photo batch export and single-video export, fewer mistakes bridging the graded preview into export defaults, aligned edit/export chrome, a searchable preset picker, and automatic video preview pause while export is busy.

webFilmLabPreview033.title: Web demo preview tuning (v0.3)
webFilmLabPreview033.description: Adjusted preview sizing and media presentation in the browser demo for a closer match to Desktop.

desktopFilmProcess040.title: Desktop v0.4 — film process controls
desktopFilmProcess040.description: Compression, compression range, print contrast, and cyan / magenta / yellow trim — aligned between the browser demo preview and Desktop export.

quickProFilmStock040.title: Quick / Pro layout and Film Stock picker (v0.4)
quickProFilmStock040.description: Quick stays on the shortest path; Pro exposes process, artifacts, source trim, and LUT in order. Preset surfaces group film stocks with clearer boundaries (including stocks like Velvia 50).

videoTransport042.title: Video preview transport (v0.4.2)
videoTransport042.description: Play/pause, timeline scrub, timecode, and Space to toggle playback on Web and Desktop — with locks during export or preview hold, and safe interaction alongside Compare mode.

proPanelVocabulary042.title: Pro panel vocabulary & inline hints (v0.4.2)
proPanelVocabulary042.description: Clearer Pro labels (film texture, source adjustments, color fringing), improved Japanese for Bloom/Halation, hover hints on collapsible headers, and a Bloom threshold tooltip.

fasterVideoExport043.title: Faster export for heavy codec sources (v0.4.3)
fasterVideoExport043.description: 4K HEVC and other heavy format sources are automatically optimized before export, delivering up to 4× faster throughput.

progressivePreview051.title: Progressive preview for heavy footage (v0.5.1)
progressivePreview051.description: Heavy formats such as ProRes and 4K HEVC now open with an immediate native-decoded preview, then switch over to an optimized intermediate in the background for smoother work.

portraitMotionBlur051.title: Portrait video + rebuilt motion blur (v0.5.1)
portraitMotionBlur051.description: Vertical footage now displays in full-frame contain mode, and motion blur has been rebuilt around an eight-frame ring buffer with shutter-angle control.

crossFilter060.title: Cross Filter optical effect (v0.6.0)
crossFilter060.description: A new diffraction-style star filter for bright point lights, with controls for strength, point count, rotation, streak length, threshold, and chromatic split.

proxyCacheAndVideoUx060.title: Proxy cache and video UX polish (v0.6.0)
proxyCacheAndVideoUx060.description: Desktop now keeps progressive preview proxies in a bounded local cache, while compare dismissal, faster playback review, slider reset discoverability, and thumbnail/loading polish have all been improved.

desktopPolish061.title: Desktop stability and look polish (v0.6.1)
desktopPolish061.description: The launch-time update banner is back, preview recovery after export is more reliable, glow was retuned for black-mist night scenes, and hard cross-filter spacing now behaves more predictably.

crossFilterCleanup062.title: Cross Filter product-surface cleanup (v0.6.2)
crossFilterCleanup062.description: The public product surface now freezes Soft mode, normalises restored and shared state back to Hard, and replaces the old Spikes slider with direct 4 / 6 / 8 choices.

webgpuPreview100.title: Desktop v1.0 — WebGPU preview backend
webgpuPreview100.description: Desktop preview now runs on a WebGPU path with wider highlight headroom, and Cross Filter ships live on that preview path with inline threshold, chromatic, and spacing controls.

presetExpansion.title: Preset expansion
presetExpansion.description: Additional film stocks and creative looks beyond the initial four.

exportQuality.title: Preview/export parity for video and batch
exportQuality.description: Bring video export and batch output closer to the new WebGPU preview path so highlight rolloff and overall rendering match more reliably.

verticalVideoExportQuality.title: Portrait & non-16:9 video export resolution
verticalVideoExportQuality.description: Improving scaling so vertical sources are less likely to be shrunk more than needed, using a long-edge-oriented cap.

smartLookAi.title: Smart Look AI
smartLookAi.description: AI-assisted image correction on Desktop — adjusts photos to better suit the chosen preset's look. Desktop-first; Web may follow later.

dngRawSupport.title: DNG / RAW support
dngRawSupport.description: Import and grade raw files directly without prior conversion.

windowsSupport.title: Windows support
windowsSupport.description: Bring Filmtone Desktop to Windows for broader accessibility.

lutExport.title: External editor handoff (under evaluation)
lutExport.description: Exploring a handoff path for Filmtone grades. No public format or editor workflow is promised until it ships.

filmDeveloperFuture.title: Film-style develop step (under evaluation)
filmDeveloperFuture.description: Exploring whether a dedicated develop-style stage fits Filmtone. Not included in v0.4; timing and scope are TBD.

mobileApp.title: Mobile app
mobileApp.description: A lightweight mobile companion for quick grading on the go.

cloudSync.title: Cloud preset sync
cloudSync.description: Sync your custom presets across Desktop, Web, and Mobile.

pluginIntegration.title: Editor plugin integration
pluginIntegration.description: Integrate Filmtone presets directly into photo and video editing apps.

roadmap.disclaimer: This roadmap reflects our current plans and may change. Items in Planned and Considering are not commitments.

releaseNotes.title: Release Notes — Filmtone
releaseNotes.description: Filmtone public release history for Desktop and iPhone — see what's new, fixed, and improved in each public version.
releaseNotes.heroBody: Desktop and iPhone ship on separate rails. This page shows only public releases; unreleased iPhone candidates stay in App Store Connect and fastlane metadata until they are live.

platformIntro.desktop: macOS public releases distributed as signed and notarized DMGs.
platformIntro.ios: Public App Store releases for the iPhone app. Unreleased local candidates are intentionally not listed here.

entries.v18Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.8 — 24fps Slow Mode and native export contracts
entries.v18SlowMode: Sources above 24fps can now export through 24fps Slow Mode. Filmtone writes a slower 24fps output and records timing metadata in the sidecar so the export choice remains recoverable.
entries.v18FilmBreath: Film Breath is now part of the shared native color contract. The default path remains neutral, while stronger settings can produce controlled temporal modulation in native export paths.
entries.v18BlackFloorControls: blackPoint and toeContrast now travel through the shared TypeScript and Swift contracts, giving the grade path an explicit low-end anchor without a sidecar schema bump.
entries.v18AutomationPath: The Codex-facing automation path now uses the native automation CLI and MCP server with bounded paths, preview-before-run batch plans, signed plan checks, and clearer unsupported-profile errors. It is workflow automation, not an in-app chat surface.
entries.v17Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.7 — audio-preserving export and Texture Softness
entries.v17AudioExport: Normal video export now reads the source audio track, writes AAC audio into the MP4, and validates the completed file before reporting success.
entries.v17TextureSoftness: Advanced Optics now includes Texture Softness, a control for easing hard digital fine detail separately from Lens Softness.
entries.v17SourceDetailCompensation: Preview and export paths can apply a conservative runtime-only detail bias when source metadata suggests heavily sharpened consumer footage. The bias is not saved into Looks.
entries.v17HighlightReelAudioLimit: Highlight-reel export remains source-audio disabled because those clips are rebuilt from selected timeline segments.
entries.v16Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.6 — right-rail reachability and surface cleanup
entries.v16RightRailReach: The right inspector rail now reaches close to the bottom of the window even while a video is loaded. The scrub bar reserves space for the rail instead of sitting underneath it, so lower controls such as Export remain reachable.
entries.v16RightRailHitDeadZone: Fixed the lower-half hit dead zone in the right rail. Hover, click, drag, and scroll now work from top to bottom while preserving the Apple Liquid Glass control styling.
entries.v16OpeningBackdrop: The empty opening state now shows the Filmtone mark and instruction copy without the central open CTA. Open media from the toolbar Open button or Command-O. Loaded media uses a media-derived blurred backdrop instead of a flat black matte.
entries.v16IntensityRow: Backlight Veil Intensity now appears only when a 1/8, 1/4, or 1/2 density chip is selected, so the None state no longer leaves a disabled-looking slider in the panel.
entries.v15Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.5 — portrait editing, Backlight Veil, and Look Strength
entries.v15PortraitVideoEditing: Portrait video keeps the clip as the primary surface while the right inspector rail and two-row scrub bar keep playback, markers, speed, and export controls reachable.
entries.v15BacklightVeilIntensity: Backlight Veil gained a continuous Intensity cursor threaded through still preview, video preview, still export, video export, scrub thumbnails, and sidecar output.
entries.v15LookStrength: Look Strength now drives Creative LUT alpha continuously, so Stone and Urban respond naturally across the slider range.
entries.v15HighlightReelFoundation: Highlight markers can now resolve to source-relative one-second clip segments through the shared Swift core contract used by Native Desktop, iPhone, and DaVinci.
entries.v14Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.4 — Native Desktop replacement cutover
entries.v14NativeDesktopCutover: The public Desktop rail moved from the Electron app to the macOS 26+ Native Desktop app while keeping the existing Bundle ID and update path.
entries.v14LiquidGlassControls: Toolbar, sidebar, inspector, picker, menus, scrub bar, and editing panels were rebuilt as Apple Liquid Glass control surfaces while keeping the preview content layer glass-free for color judgment.
entries.v14StillVideoExport: Still and video open, preview, export, and sidecar paths now run inside the native app using the Filmtone grade path aligned with the iPhone app.
entries.v14LegacyElectronFrozen: Desktop v1.0.4 remains available as the frozen legacy build for pre-macOS-26 users; new Desktop product work now belongs to Native Desktop.
entries.v104Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.0.4 — Log Conversion profiles and finishing parity
entries.v104LogConversionProfiles: Desktop Log Conversion now includes built-in Camera Profile choices for Rec.709, Apple Log, Apple Log 2, DJI D-Log, DJI D-Log M, Canon C-Log, Canon Log 3 / Cinema Gamut, Panasonic V-Log, and Sony S-Log3, while keeping custom .cube imports available.
entries.v104SourceProfileSidecars: Export sidecars can preserve built-in source-profile identity, so reopening a session can regenerate the matching conversion LUT from the catalog instead of depending on the original absolute .cube path.
entries.v104FinishingCatalog: Desktop carries the current shared finishing catalog, including newer Creative LUT data, Stone and Urban refinements, Lens Filter profiles, and renderer-side motion, glow, halation, diffusion, and optical shader updates.
entries.v104Terminology: Desktop-facing copy now follows the current Filmtone terminology pass for effect names, HDR messages, and shared product language.
entries.v103Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.0.3 — export quality and HDR source handling
entries.v103HdrHandling: HDR PQ, HLG, and wide-gamut source detection is clearer during import and export, with user-facing messages that explain practical brightness or color risk without developer jargon.
entries.v103BundledVideoTools: Desktop now bundles the video toolchain needed for normal exports, reducing dependency on separate developer or Homebrew setup for HDR-to-SDR preparation paths.
entries.v103PreviewExportTrust: Video export starts closer to the visible preview grade, keeps trusted source frame rate and geometry, and writes full-range BT.709 output so mist, bloom, halation, and highlight rolloff shift less at encode time.
entries.v103DefaultLook: New sessions and old grade imports without preset identity now start from Neutral / Clean Base with the shared soft-finish baseline.
entries.v102Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.0.2 — safer video export recovery
entries.v102FfmpegPipeRecovery: Broken ffmpeg pipe failures are caught and surfaced through the normal export failure path instead of leaving the renderer waiting on stale writes.
entries.v102ExportSessionIsolation: Each video export now has its own session id, so stale start, frame, finish, or abort messages from older exports cannot affect the active job.
entries.v102PreviewExportTrust: The current WebGPU preview/export contract stays aligned while export hardening continues, including low-end grain and offscreen render refinements.
entries.v101Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.0.1 — preview trust and cleaner write-out
entries.v101HighlightPreview: Bright footage is steadier in preview, with highlights that hold their shape more naturally while you judge the finished mood.
entries.v101CrossFilterPreview: Cross Filter is easier to tune live, with more reliable brightness onset, chromatic split, and spacing behavior on moving footage.
entries.v101ExportSidecar: Desktop exports can write a .filmtone-session.json sidecar so the finishing setup can be inspected, saved, and reopened later.
entries.v101WriteOutSurface: The write-out tab uses a cleaner glass surface with clearer controls, fields, preset tiles, and dividers.
entries.v100Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.0 — the first public release
entries.v100WebgpuPreview: Preview has been reworked end-to-end. Bright highlights now hold their shape more naturally, so it is easier to judge the finished look right on screen.
entries.v100CrossFilterPreviewControls: Cross Filter now responds live while you preview your image. Fine-tune the brightness that triggers the streaks, how much they split into color, and how close they sit, and the result updates immediately.
entries.v100SignedNotarizedDmg: The macOS build is now signed and notarized by Apple. The download page and the in-app update prompt both point to this v1.0.0 release, so installing is simple and trusted.
entries.v100DesktopFirstReleaseScope: v1.0 focuses on improving Desktop preview. The browser demo, video export, and photo batch export continue to work exactly as they did before.
entries.v062HardOnlySurface: Cross Filter now ships as a single, well-tuned mode, trimmed down so it is easier to reach for without hesitation.
entries.v062StateNormalization: Old settings files and shared links open correctly and automatically fit into the current mode — nothing looks different from what you originally saved.
entries.v062DiscreteSpikes: Pick the number of streaks in one tap: 4, 6, or 8.
entries.v061Title: Update notifications are back, and night-scene glow feels better
entries.v061LaunchUpdateBanner: Filmtone again shows a banner at launch when a newer version is available.
entries.v061PreviewRecoveryAfterExport: Fixed cases where preview could stay black after exporting — preview now recovers on its own whenever it is needed.
entries.v061GlowBlackMistRetune: Glow in Black-Mist-style night scenes now keeps its shape instead of flattening into blown-out white patches.
entries.v061HardCrossFilterSpacing: Cross Filter streaks now separate cleanly even when bright highlights sit close together.
entries.v060Title: Cross Filter arrives, and video feels smoother
entries.v060CrossFilter: Cross Filter adds lens-style star streaks to bright points in your image. Dial in the strength, the number of streaks, the angle, the length, the brightness that triggers them, and a touch of color split, to find your own look.
entries.v060VideoCompareUx: Video compare and review feel smoother — compare mode is easier to exit, slider resets are easier to find, and a faster playback option makes quick checks more natural.
entries.v060ThumbnailLoadingPolish: Leading thumbnails now pick a brighter frame automatically, so clips that fade in look right from the very first glance. Loading text has also been aligned with the rest of the app.
entries.v060PersistentProxyCache: Desktop can now keep preview data for heavy footage on your computer, so opening the same clip again is faster. You can let Filmtone manage the space automatically or clear it yourself whenever you want.
entries.v051ProgressiveLoading: ProRes, 4K HEVC, and other demanding formats preview the moment you drop them in. Filmtone prepares an optimized copy in the background and reuses it at export, so you never wait on the same clip twice.
entries.v051RingBufferMotionBlur: Motion blur has been rebuilt with real shutter-angle control (0° to 720°), and a separate Trail Intensity slider for stylised streaks, so you can shape the look more intuitively.
entries.v051PortraitVideo: 9:16 vertical clips now display full-frame. The side areas are filled with a softly blurred version of the footage itself, so portrait video looks polished without any manual setup.
entries.v051ComparisonModeFix: Fixed Before / After compare so only the graded side shows motion blur — the original stays clean, and no ghost frames carry over when you switch modes.
entries.v050Title: Grain that looks like the real thing
entries.v050GrainV3: The grain engine has been rebuilt from the ground up — each film stock now has its own natural clumping, texture size, and color-noise character, so Kodak and Fuji grain no longer look the same.
entries.v050Diffusion: A new Diffusion slider wraps your image in a soft, milky haze — like shooting through a Pro-Mist filter — gently lifting contrast and flattering skin tones.
entries.v050CineStillHalation: CineStill 800T now loads clean by default. Dial in the iconic red halation glow yourself with the slider whenever you want it.
entries.v050PresetRecalibration: All 10 film stock presets have been hand-tuned with matching grain size and diffusion, so each look feels true to the actual film it was inspired by.
entries.v050UiReorganization: The Pro panel has been reorganized so the controls you use most are immediately visible. Effects still being refined are tucked away until they are ready.
entries.v045BloomHalationRework: Bloom and halation have been completely reimagined — glow spreads more naturally, highlights behave at any slider position, and the overall look is closer to real film. Existing grades may shift slightly.
entries.v045PresetRecalibration: All 10 film stock presets have been recalibrated so bloom and halation feel natural and true to each stock's character.
entries.v044ProresLoadAndExport: You can now import, grade, and export ProRes MOV files — including LOG footage straight from your camera. Filmtone prepares the file automatically on the way in.
entries.v044Dci4kInput: Cinema-resolution files (DCI 4K and above) are now fully supported as video input.
entries.v043FasterHevcExport: 4K footage that used to take three minutes to export now finishes in under 45 seconds — up to 4× faster for demanding camera files.
entries.v043AutoSourceOptimize: Filmtone quietly optimizes heavy camera files before grading so export runs at full speed. Lighter files skip this step entirely.
entries.v043OptimizationProgress: A progress bar now shows while Filmtone prepares a heavy source file, so you know exactly what is happening before export begins.
entries.v042ProPanelVocabulary: Pro panel labels have been updated to plain photography language — Film texture, Color fringing, Source adjustments — so controls are easier to understand at a glance.
entries.v042BloomThresholdHint: Bloom's threshold slider now shows a brief tip explaining which highlight tones trigger the glow.
entries.v042VideoTransport: Video preview now has full playback controls — play, pause, scrub, timecode display, and Space bar toggle.
entries.v041ProToneLabels: The tone section now uses everyday language — highlight softness, tone span, print snap — with short hover descriptions so every slider is self-explanatory.
entries.v041SliderTooltipReset: All sliders now show a tip reminding you that tapping the label resets that control to default.
entries.v040Title: Film process controls and a cleaner workflow
entries.v040FilmProcess: New film process controls let you shape compression, tonal range, print contrast, and color cast — what you see in the preview is exactly what exports.
entries.v040QuickProIa: Quick mode takes you straight to the look; Pro mode surfaces the full set of film process, texture, and source controls — each mode shows only what you need.
entries.v040FilmStockPicker: Film stocks are now grouped by category, so finding Velvia 50 among cinematic and other options takes seconds instead of scrolling.
entries.v040PanelStability: Desktop no longer loses your process settings when you switch between photo and video tabs.
entries.v040ShareCompat: Shared links and exported grades remain fully compatible with older versions while carrying the new process fields when available.
entries.v031Title: Export in the browser — and better reliability across the board
entries.v031WebVideoExportBeta: You can now export a graded video clip directly from the browser — no download required to test your look on short footage.
entries.v031WebBrowserReliability: Browser export is more reliable, and a clearer message now guides Safari users toward Chrome, Edge, or the Desktop app when needed.
entries.v031FinderThumb: Exported MP4s no longer show a black thumbnail in Finder or Quick Look — previews now display the actual graded frame.
entries.v031MovHandling: Video import now handles a wider range of camera files, including MOV files that some cameras save without standard type information.
entries.v030Title: Cleaner export and faster preset discovery
entries.v030ExportIa: Photo batch export and single video export are now clearly separated — tabs, panel, and toolbar all point you to the right place.
entries.v030ExportSource: The image or clip you are actively grading carries over into export as the default, so wrong-file exports are much less likely.
entries.v030VisualPolish: The export panel and the editing view share the same visual language, making the transition between grading and exporting feel seamless.
entries.v030PresetSearch: Type to search film stock presets — no more scrolling through the full list to find a specific look.
entries.v030ExportBusyPause: Video preview pauses automatically while a file is exporting so nothing looks out of sync.
entries.v030WebPreview: The browser demo preview is taller and better framed, giving a closer impression of the Desktop experience.
entries.v020Title: Two LUTs at once, redesigned export, and faster video
entries.v020DualLut: Load two LUT files simultaneously — use the first to convert your LOG footage to a standard look, the second for your creative grade, each with its own intensity control.
entries.v020LutSync: LUTs you set in the editing tab now follow through to export. A status indicator shows at a glance whether your grade is in sync, out of sync, or partially applied.
entries.v020InlineExportPanel: Export now lives right alongside your grade in a compact panel — the image stays visible the whole time, no more multi-step wizard.
entries.v020WebCodecsReEnabled: Video export in the browser has been restored with improved color accuracy and hardware-accelerated performance.
entries.v020UpdateNotify: A banner appears inside the app when a new version of Filmtone is available.
entries.v020PackageRefactor: Under-the-hood restructuring to keep the app fast and stable as new features are added.
entries.v013FrameLogSuppression: Video export now runs more cleanly in the background, with a small performance improvement on longer clips.
entries.v012VideoColorShift: Fixed a color shift that could appear in exported video, ensuring graded footage matches what you see on screen.
entries.v011FfmpegPath: Fixed an issue where the Desktop app (DMG) could fail to process video after installation.
entries.v010BatchExport: Apply any preset to an entire folder of photos and export them all at once as JPEG or PNG.
entries.v010VideoExport: Export a video clip with your chosen grade baked in.
entries.v010FourPresets: Four film stock looks to start: Kodak Portra 400, Fuji Pro 400H, Kodak Ektar 100, and Ilford HP5 Plus.
entries.v010BrowserDemo: Try any preset on your own photos in the browser before downloading the Desktop app.
entries.iosV18Title: Filmtone for iPhone v1.8 — capture flow and take selection
entries.iosV18ContinuousCapture: Keep recording multiple takes, then choose the take to open in the editor from a focused preview.
entries.iosV18CaptureMonitorMode: When stabilization and a Look are active together, capture uses a lighter monitor view while editing and export keep the full-quality render path.
entries.iosV18CaptureLooks: Stone, Urban, Noir, and imported .cube creative LUTs can be selected from the capture screen, with the selected direction carried into editing and export.
entries.iosV18CaptureStability: Capture orientation, low-storage warnings, and capture package stability were tightened.
entries.iosV12Title: Filmtone for iPhone v1.2 — stronger LUT and export stability
entries.iosV12DualLutControls: Source Profile and Film Look now work as two separate .cube LUT paths, each with 0-100% intensity control.
entries.iosV12PreviewExportColor: Preview and export color processing are better aligned, so exported media stays closer to what you checked on screen.
entries.iosV12HdrP3Handling: P3 / HDR media handling avoids unsafe intermediate paths and keeps source handling more stable.
entries.iosV12CacheProtection: Cache cleanup protects unsaved exports and active work while removing older temporary files.
entries.iosV11Title: Filmtone for iPhone v1.1 — source transparency
entries.iosV11HdrNotice: HDR and wide-gamut clips now show an in-app notice so you can see how iOS will handle the source before export.
entries.iosV11OpticsMetadata: Camera and optics metadata can feed the vignette model for more physically accurate corner falloff on supported clips.
entries.iosV11SidecarJson: Exports include a sidecar JSON alongside the media with grade, preset, and camera context for cleaner round trips with Desktop.
entries.iosV11ProresAppleLog: ProRes and Apple Log import handling is clearer, and unsupported conversion paths are recorded in the sidecar instead of being hidden.
entries.iosV10Title: Filmtone for iPhone v1.0 — first App Store release
entries.iosV10Presets: Film-stock presets are available on iPhone as the starting point for quick local grading.
entries.iosV10QuickControls: Quick controls cover exposure, contrast, and saturation for fast adjustment on the device.
entries.iosV10DualLut: Camera Profile and Film Look LUT slots support more precise source and creative workflows.
entries.iosV10ExportShare: Export, save to Photos, and share are available from the iPhone workflow.

metadata.title: Filmtone iPhone Privacy
metadata.description: Privacy summary for Filmtone on iPhone: local-first operation, no account, no analytics SDK, no third-party tracking, and no data collection.

privacyPage.heroBody: Filmtone on iPhone is local-first. The app does not require an account, does not include analytics or third-party tracking SDKs, and does not collect your photos, videos, or usage data.

facts.localFirstValue: Editing, preview, and export run on your device.
facts.noAccountValue: No sign-in, no profile, no cloud sync requirement.
facts.noAnalyticsValue: No analytics SDK. No ad-tech SDK.
facts.noCollectionValue: No collected data types. No third-party tracking.

localFirst.title: Editing stays on your iPhone
localFirst.body: This release keeps the media workflow on device. The app is designed to work without an account or cloud processing.

editing.title: Editing runs locally
editing.body: Applying looks, generating previews, and exporting media happen on the iPhone itself.

storage.title: Working files stay on device

portfolio-renewal-2026.title: Giving up dark/light dual-mode — how a WebGPU shader's hardcoded value chose the entire site's palette
portfolio-renewal-2026.summary: Unifying the portfolio's background to a single sheet was, in fact, decided by the technology from the start. A WebGPU-driven motion-dot shader bakes its clear color as `[0.82, 0.82, 0.82, 1.0]`, so any divergence from that value flickers the background on every scroll. The dual-mode path was already closed. This is a record of accepting that constraint as a method — and what we cut to make it work (CSS scrims, theme toggles, full-surface Liquid Glass).
portfolio-renewal-2026.metaDescription: An editorial record of dropping dark/light dual-mode in favor of a single light substrate. Starting from a WebGPU shader's hardcoded constraint, readability moved into the shader pipeline itself, with cut features and preserved exceptions made explicit.

mobile-safari-touch-controller.title: Solving iOS Safari's 100vh problem with a single CSS variable — why we lower visualViewport into :root
mobile-safari-touch-controller.summary: iOS Safari's URL bar collapse breaks `100vh`, opening gaps in the background during scroll. Distributing the value through React context or props collapsed early in an environment where SSR, client, and shaders coexist. Instead, a small client component subscribed to `window.visualViewport` writes to `:root` CSS variables (`--vvh` / `--vvw` / `--vv-offset-*`), and CSS, JSX, and shaders all read from the same source. A record of a quiet, single-source-of-truth pattern that simply does not break.
mobile-safari-touch-controller.metaDescription: How to solve iOS Safari's 100vh breakage with the `visualViewport` API published to `:root` CSS variables — a robust pattern derived from the failure of distributing the same value through React context across SSR, client, and shaders.

journal-typography-wordmark-system.title: Why our wordmark lives as SVG paths, not a font — a pipeline that re-carves only the glyphs we need from Geist Sans
journal-typography-wordmark-system.summary: Identity needed a carved wordmark, not a font. Off-the-shelf display faces couldn't reach the flat-top A, the K junction gap, or the C terminal cuts at the Bezier-control-point level. We built an extract → modify → build pipeline: it takes Geist Sans Medium 500, isolates A, K, C, T, H, B, M, modifies their letterforms, and freezes them as SVG paths. The coexistence with Jost is still unresolved — leaving that visible is part of the record.
journal-typography-wordmark-system.metaDescription: Why a portfolio wordmark lives as SVG paths rather than a font, plus the pipeline that carves only the needed glyphs out of Geist Sans. A typographic editorial choice — giving up reversibility to gain identity.

filmtone-motion-180-shutter-baseline.title: From shutter angle to exposure frame count — Filmtone's motion blur math, aligned with industry conventions
filmtone-motion-180-shutter-baseline.summary: Treating shutter angle as exposure duration. `exposureFrames = clamp(angle, 0, 720) / 360`, with 180° as the baseline (`0.5 frame`). Only `additionalExposureFrames = max(0, target - 0.5)` reaches the ring buffer. The mapping is `360° → 2 frames (triangle weights [2/3, 1/3])` and `720° → 3 frames (flat weights [1/3, 1/3, 1/3])`. The same math is shared across a WebGL fragment shader, a WebGPU compute shader, and an iOS Swift export session — and validated against RED, Foundry Nuke, Blender, Houdini, and After Effects.
filmtone-motion-180-shutter-baseline.metaDescription: Filmtone's motion blur implementation: shutter angle normalized to exposure duration, with a 180° baseline plus ring-buffer additional exposure across WebGL/WebGPU/Swift. Walks through `exposureFrames = angle/360` and the concrete weight arrays.

filmtone-dual-lut-pipeline.title: Filmtone's two-lane LUT pipeline implementation — the inputLut/creativeLut data model and intensity blending via CIColorMatrix
filmtone-dual-lut-pipeline.summary: Filmtone holds `.cube` LUTs in two slots: `inputLut` (Source Profile / Camera) and `creativeLut` (Look). The data model is `ParsedCubeLutDTO { title, size, data, intensity }` and `SerializableLutDTO { size, data, intensity }`. The export order is fixed: `input LUT → base grade → tone compression → edge optics → glow → vignette → grain → creative LUT → print`. When `intensity < 0.999`, results blend linearly via `CIColorMatrix` (source) over `CISourceOverCompositing` (LUT output); above that, the LUT output passes through. On source replacement, `inputLut` clears but `creativeLut` is preserved.
filmtone-dual-lut-pipeline.metaDescription: Implementation of Filmtone's two-lane LUT pipeline — inputLut/creativeLut data model, the fixed export order, CIColorMatrix + CISourceOverCompositing intensity blending, and the source-replacement preservation rule.

filmtone-cross-platform-color-parity.title: Generating Swift from TypeScript math — Filmtone's cross-platform color parity pipeline
filmtone-cross-platform-color-parity.summary: Color transforms, motion blur, and exposure math live in TypeScript inside `packages/film-lab-renderer/src/`. `bun run generate:filmtone-ios-swift` mechanically produces `FilmtonePhase0Generated.swift`; hand-editing the generated module is prohibited. The Phase 0 contract test (`verify:swift-contract`) confirms the generated math matches the TypeScript output. WebGL fragment shaders read the math as GLSL constants, WebGPU compute shaders as WGSL, and the iOS Swift export session as the generated module. Color parity is held by structure, not discipline.
filmtone-cross-platform-color-parity.metaDescription: How Filmtone keeps colors identical across WebGL/WebGPU preview and iOS Swift export — TypeScript as the single source of math, generated to Swift via `generate:filmtone-ios-swift` and validated through `verify:swift-contract`.

filmtone-capacitor-native-bridge.title: Reaching iOS PhotoLibrary, Core Image, and ActivityKit through a Capacitor native plugin — implementing FilmtoneMediaPlugin's nine methods
filmtone-capacitor-native-bridge.summary: Filmtone iOS is a Capacitor 7.4 hybrid app, but `FilmtoneMediaPlugin` exposes nine native methods to the TypeScript side: `pickSource` (PhotoLibrary), `pickLutFile` (DocumentPicker), `probeSource` (AVAsset metadata), `renderPreviewFrame` (Core Image), `runExport` (Core Video write), `saveToPhotos` (PHPhotoLibrary), `shareOutput` (UIActivityViewController), `cancelExport`, `handleMemoryWarning`. Each is published via Swift `@objc`, with a TypeScript proxy in `src/native/filmtoneMedia.ts`. Bridge changes ship in dual-side PRs (single-side updates are the most common runtime breakage).
filmtone-capacitor-native-bridge.metaDescription: How Filmtone iOS reaches iOS PhotoLibrary, Core Image, and ActivityKit through a Capacitor native plugin — the nine methods of `FilmtoneMediaPlugin` (pickSource / runExport / Live Activity / cancelExport, etc.) and the TS-Swift dual-PR pattern.

filmtone-app-store-v12-shipping.title: Splitting an iOS release into six fastlane lanes — Filmtone's archive / screenshots / metadata / beta / release / submit_review design
filmtone-app-store-v12-shipping.summary: Fastlane is split into six lanes by responsibility: `archive` (IPA build), `screenshots` (UI test snapshots), `metadata` (ASC localized metadata + review info), `beta` (TestFlight upload), `release` (binary + metadata + screenshots upload), `submit_review` (resubmits an existing build for review). The record covers two production traps and their fixes: gym 2.233 passing auth args into both `xcargs` and `export_xcargs` (causing `Exit status: 64` on IPA export), and deliver missing `release_notes` in upload options (causing ASC to reject the review submission for missing `whatsNew`). Each is patched with minimum-viable Fastfile edits.

motionStudies.indexTitle: Motion Studies — dissecting motion techniques, one at a time
motionStudies.indexSummary: An archive that dissects one motion technique per article, each with a live demo. It records not just how each one is built, but the attempts that were tried and cut.
motionStudies.metaDescription: Motion Studies — an R&D archive dissecting one motion technique per article, each with a live demo.

lattice-breath.title: Dissecting dots that seem to multiply
lattice-breath.summary: The dots seem to grow from 6 to 19 and fall back to 6 — yet not a single one is created. No key animates the count; it looks like more because each appearance is slightly offset in time. Layer group-staggered entrances onto the lattice's open-and-close, and the count change happens on its own. The whole trick is written out as short framework-free functions and dissected.
lattice-breath.metaDescription: A motion study of dots that appear to multiply 6→19→6 with no key animating the count. Nothing is actually created — staggered appearance timing produces the change. The short function that computes the motion is in the article, replayed live in the browser.

pulse-grid.title: Dissecting an order that looks random
pulse-grid.summary: Nine dots pop in an order you can't predict — yet no random number is drawn anywhere. The motion is one keyframed clip, replayed by all nine duplicates a fixed beat apart; the order comes from a single fixed table holding each cell's place in line. The whole build — down to the spring-like undershoot that turns out to be an authored key — is written out as short functions and dissected.
pulse-grid.metaDescription: A motion study dissecting "random": the firing order of nine dots comes from one fixed table, zero rng — a single radius-keyframe clip time-shifted by a fixed beat times its place in line, so every loop plays out exactly the same. The short function that computes the motion is in the article, replayed live in the browser.

tangency-coupled-drive.title: Dissecting a rotation that seems to stop
tangency-coupled-drive.summary: While the center square makes a quarter turn, the side squares slide as if bolted to it, and near the diamond everything seems to pause. Yet only the rotation carries keyframes — three. The sides have zero; their position is computed every frame as the closest spot that stays clear of the spinning square. Even the pause is nobody stopping anything. One rotation and a one-line contact law, written out as short functions and dissected.
tangency-coupled-drive.metaDescription: A motion study dissecting linkage: three rotation keyframes drive everything, and the side squares are computed each frame as the closest spot that stays clear of the spinning square — the apparent stop near the diamond happens because the width barely changes around the diamond, not because of a hold key. The short function that computes the motion is in the article, replayed live in the browser.

complement-tangent-pair.title: Dissecting two circles that look inversely proportional
complement-tangent-pair.summary: Two kissing circles keep trading size — one inflates exactly as the other deflates. The drawer is named "inverse proportion", yet measured, the equation where the product of the radii stays constant does not hold. What stays constant is the addition: the radii always sum to the same number. Keyframes sit only on the top-left circle's radius — 3 of them; the other radius is a subtraction from that sum, and both centres are computed to recede from a fixed kiss point by their own radius, so the contact never moves through the whole loop. The whole build is written out as short framework-free functions and dissected.
complement-tangent-pair.metaDescription: A motion study dissecting two circles that look inversely proportional: what stays constant is the radius sum, not the product — the constant-product equation misses an order of magnitude worse than the constant-sum one. 3 keyframes on one radius, a subtraction from that sum for its partner, centres computed from a fixed contact point so the kiss never drifts. The short function that computes the motion is in the article, replayed live in the browser.

master-rotation-echo.title: Dissecting dots that seem to trail
master-rotation-echo.summary: While 2 dots make one lap around a circle, the tail splits into flip-book frames in the fast stretch, melts into one band in the slow stretch, and vanishes the moment they stop. Yet only one rotation is animated — every layer of the tail is the dot's own past, the same rotation replayed a fixed beat later per copy. And nobody switches between the split and the melt, either. One rotation and 9 copies, written out as short functions and dissected.
master-rotation-echo.metaDescription: A motion study dissecting the afterimage: one animated rotation, and a tail of 9 copies replaying it one fixed delay apart — whether the tail reads as flip-book frames or melts into one band depends only on whether the dot outruns its own width within one copy's delay. The short function that computes the motion is in the article, replayed live in the browser.

shared-hold-pulse.title: Dissecting 5 shapes that seem choreographed
shared-hold-pulse.summary: 4 bars stretch open to the left and right, the center square swells, all of them freeze together at full stretch for a beat, then walk the same road home. They look perfectly rehearsed, yet not one shape has its own keyframes — the only thing animated is a single number that climbs from 0 to 1, pauses, and returns to 0. Every shape just reads that number times its own motion amount; the mirror is nothing but the sign flipping between left and right. The center square even makes a half turn on the same number. One number and a table of motion amounts, written out as short functions and dissected.
shared-hold-pulse.metaDescription: A motion study dissecting the symmetry drawer: one number that climbs from 0 to 1, holds, and returns drives 4 mirrored bars and a half-turning center square at once — no per-shape keyframes; the mirror is just a sign flip between left and right. The short function that computes the motion is in the article, replayed live in the browser.

whip-crawl-path-cycle.title: Dissecting a lap that seems to shift gears
whip-crawl-path-cycle.summary: A thick stroke's head and its dot sprint through most of a lap of an ∞ track in one burst, then crawl the rest. It looks like a two-gear lap, but you choose just 2 speed keys — one whip's worth; the crawl's speed follows automatically from the promise that one loop closes exactly 1 lap. The line never stretches: a fixed-length window slides along the track.
whip-crawl-path-cycle.metaDescription: A motion study dissecting the drawer technique 'cycle'. The two-gear pacing of a dot lapping an ∞ track is one cubic-bezier whip plus the crawl left over by the promise of closing the lap — no gearbox anywhere. The stroke is a fixed-length dash window sliding on the path. The short function that computes the motion is in the article, replayed live in the browser.

signal-stroke-relay.title: The relay sensation cannot be built from separate animations — a Theatre.js timeline referenced by multiple layers with phase offsets
signal-stroke-relay.summary: The feeling of "a single motion traveling across layers" disappears the moment you write separate animations per layer. It only emerges when multiple layers reference the same motion with different offsets and eases. We held a single Theatre.js timeline as the "stem" of the gesture, with each layer reading it as its own "dialect" — a record of that structure.
signal-stroke-relay.metaDescription: A motion study on building the relay sensation — multiple layers referencing one Theatre.js timeline with phase-offset eases — and why separate animations cannot reach it.

staged-emphasis-payoff.title: How to keep a payoff in a three-line headline reveal — give the last stage a different ease
staged-emphasis-payoff.summary: Three lines on the same ease arrive together and the meaning scatters. Three lines on three different eases overwhelm and the weight becomes unreadable. Bind them as a family, assign them to early / mid / late stages, and reserve a different ease for the final stage — the payoff. We cap the number of stages at three. A pacing study with that constraint as the design.
staged-emphasis-payoff.metaDescription: A motion study on pacing three-line headline reveals — using the family / stage / payoff vocabulary, with a separate ease reserved for the final stage.

boiling-poster-aperture.title: A poster reveal that feels like wet paper — a boil noise that displaces only the rim (touch the interior and the paper-feel collapses)
boiling-poster-aperture.summary: A CSS clip-path reveals a poster with mechanical, hard edges. For a paper-like bleed, we hold a time-evolving boil field as low-frequency noise in WebGL and use it to displace only the mask's rim. The interior moves zero pixels. The counterintuitive rule: displace the interior even slightly, and paper turns to jelly.
boiling-poster-aperture.metaDescription: A motion study on revealing a poster with paper-like bleed using a boil noise field and displacement — confined to the rim only, with the interior held completely still as a counterintuitive rule.

temporal-echo-residue.title: Keeping a stopped motion's echo alive at 5–10% opacity — designing residue without collapsing into VFX
temporal-echo-residue.summary: We write the subjective feeling of "the screen has stopped, but something is still moving" as a mechanism. The last N frames are held in a buffer and decay exponentially, contributing 5–10% to the shader output. Push it to 20% and the editorial frame collapses into VFX, drawing attention away from the lead motion. Hold the echo internally; restrain how much of it is visible.
temporal-echo-residue.metaDescription: A motion study on designing residue — keeping the echo of a stopped motion alive in the shader output at 5–10% mix, with a hard cap to prevent collapse into VFX.

sections.text: Why we collapsed to a single light substrate

The first decision in Renewal 2026 was to make the background one. Not a dark/light pair, not a per-section theme. A single light substrate sits underneath, and reading, work, and motion all have to live on top of it.

The reason starts on the technical side. The motion-dot background runs WebGPU and writes its own clear color every frame to hold 60fps. That clear color is float-typed and hard-coded to `[0.82, 0.82, 0.82, 1.0]`. If the site disagreed with that color, the screen would flicker between two stages on every scroll.

// packages/motion-dot/src/main.ts
bgColor: [0.82, 0.82, 0.82, 1.0]

Which means a dark site is not on the table — not without rewriting the shader pipeline. Whether you call that a constraint or a stance is a matter of attitude. I chose the second. Holding every category on a single light surface was a stronger editorial position than producing a dark mode would have been.
Readability lives in a shader, not in a CSS scrim

Light text on a moving dot field gets noisy. The first attempt was the obvious one — drop a translucent panel under each block via `::before`. Readable, but lethal as an editorial surface. Every section gained a visible rectangle.

The fix lived in the shader. Sections opt-in via `data-readability`. `useReadabilityRegions` watches them through IntersectionObserver, weights by visible area, and lerps the dominant scalar into a CSS variable `--motion-dot-readability`. The motion-dot fragment pipeline reads that scalar and dims itself. CSS covers nothing.

<header data-readability="focus">…</header>
<section data-readability="reading">…</section>
After that, the rectangles were gone. The text and the background sit on the same plane — the background just gets quieter where reading is happening.
Liquid Glass stays, but only on the chrome

We banned `backdrop-filter` from body content as a rule. The navigation chrome, on the other hand, kept its Liquid Glass — it reads visualViewport and refracts. Glass belongs to the moving subject, not to the page. It never lands on top of reading.
Body uses the data-readability shader pipeline. Chrome uses Liquid Glass. Splitting them physically meant their responsibilities stopped colliding.
What was cut

items: The dark/light dual mode toggle (lost its meaning the moment substrate became one)
Section-level glass scrims (readability moved to the shader scalar)
Decorative panels and gradient overlays in body content
Per-section route-accent variations (only the chrome accent remains)

sections.text: Exceptions kept on purpose

Filmtone and Photography stay on their own systems. Filmtone is, as a product, a dark-UI app — it scopes itself with `.dark`. Photography would be eaten by its own imagery on a light substrate, so we flip the surface locally with `body:has(.photography-page)`. These are explicit exceptions, not omissions.
What is still open
motion-dot is WebGPU-first; the WebGL2 fallback gives up density. Whether a thinner background on lower-end devices reads as 'natural' or as 'weak' isn't fully decided yet.

The other open question is what happens the day a 'night chapter' has to enter the site. Today there is no such plan, but partitioning the substrate later would be a major rebuild. I'm leaving this here as acknowledged debt.
The problem

iOS Safari grows and shrinks its URL bar with scroll. `100vh` resolves to the expanded height and freezes there. By itself that's tolerable; in practice the body height, the motion-dot canvas full-bleed, and the Liquid Glass chrome's fixed position all start moving on different bases.

The visible failure is that, the moment the URL bar collapses, the motion-dot leaves a 64-px strip of empty space at the bottom. A background that doesn't reach the bottom of the page is editorially fatal.
The fix — publish once, consume from CSS variables
The implementation is intentionally small. A single client component, `VisualViewportVars`, subscribes to `window.visualViewport` and writes the values straight onto `:root` as CSS variables.

The motion-dot canvas reads `height: var(--vvh)` directly. The Liquid Glass chrome's fixed top becomes `top: calc(var(--vv-offset-top, 0px) + 1rem)`. Neither knows about the other; both fall from the same source of truth.
Where safe-area meets it

Notch and home-indicator insets come from `env(safe-area-inset-*)` — a separate axis from visualViewport. Only header and footer padding consume it; the motion-dot canvas explicitly extends past safe-area to fill the screen. The two systems are kept apart on purpose.
What this note does not cover

This piece covers visual-viewport delivery and the safe-area boundary only. A 44-pixel touch target audit and the touch-version of the keyboard-only HUDs are separate R&D and are not yet in source. They will be written up in the next wave.

items: Comprehensive 44-pixel touch target audit (audit tool not yet built)
Touch versions of keyboard-only HUDs in Filmtone and the experiments
Cross-checking visualViewport behavior on Android Chrome

sections.text: What we learned

Putting one global source of truth on `:root` as CSS variables is unsexy and durable. Shaders read it, JSX reads it, layouts read it. As more layers were added, nothing fell out of sync. Distributing the same values via React context or props broke far more often.
Why a wordmark at all

The C-arc + 工 logomark was designed as a modern personal kamon and works at small to medium sizes. It loses force when an editorial hero needs to fill a hero band and announce whose site this is. That role belongs to a different typographic device.
Two paths: (1) drop in an off-the-shelf display face, or (2) take a base typeface and carve it into a wordmark of our own. The first is fast but anonymous. We chose the second.
The pipeline — extract, modify, build

items: extract-glyphs.ts — extracts only the glyphs needed for CHIBA / TAKUMI from Geist Sans Medium 500 (.otf) as SVG paths
modify-glyphs.ts — applies hand-picked carvings: A flat-top, K junction gap, C terminal cuts, T extension, H optical center, B ink trap, M thinning
build-wordmark.ts — composes the modified paths into CHIBA / TAKUMI and writes them into `branding.wordmark.{primaryPaths,secondaryPaths}` in `portfolio.ts`

sections.text: At runtime, `BrandWordmark` renders the path arrays as fill-based SVG. Color is `currentColor`; weight and color stay in CSS.
Why path-baked, not font-subset

A subsetted web font is still a font — moving a single vertex isn't an option. SVG paths give you a flat A top, a junction gap on K, terminal cuts on C, all as ordinary math on Bezier control points. Reversibility is lost; uniqueness is the trade.
Honesty about the in-progress part

As of Renewal 2026, Jost is not fully removed. `apps/web/src/app/fonts.ts` still exports Jost 800, referenced inside `--font-family-display`. `font-mono` usages also remain. The full migration to a single display family is queued for the next wave.

The wordmark is therefore a first step. The logotype layer was rebuilt in isolation, ahead of the broader typography clean-up that has yet to land. Writing it down while it is still in motion is the point of this study.
What it taught us

items: The base face shapes how much carving room you get. Geist's neutrality made it pleasant to modify
Carvings should be intentional and few — A and K were touched, O and U were left alone, fixed at the start
Persist outputs in a form the site can actually draw. Not .otf, not .woff2 — SVG path data inside the data layer

sections.text: Treating shutter angle as exposure duration

Normal iPhone and cinema footage is captured with roughly 180° of shutter motion blur already baked in. Filmtone Motion is an additive post process; piling another 180° pass on top of that produces visible double-blur ghosting. So Filmtone treats 180° as the no-op baseline, and only opens the target shutter window past that.
Exposure-frame normalization

Shutter angle is normalized to exposure duration per frame. `MOTION_BLUR_BASELINE_SHUTTER_ANGLE = 180` is fixed at 0.5 frame, and `MOTION_BLUR_MAX_SHUTTER_ANGLE = 720` caps the input at 2.0 frames. Only the additional exposure relative to the source is fed into the ring buffer: `additionalExposureFrames = max(0, target - 0.5)`. For `shutterAngle <= 180` this is always `0`, so preview, desktop export, and iOS export all return the spatial grade output as-is.
Active frame count — held to a short history window

The active frame count for the ring-buffer approximation is `1 + ceil(additionalExposureFrames)`, clamped to `[2, slots]`. With the default 8 slots: `360°→2 frames`, `540°→3 frames`, `720°→3 frames`. The substantive change relative to the previous `(additionalAngle / 360) * (slots / 2)` formula was replacing the `720°→6 frames` mapping; the old version became a long-tail echo rather than a shutter-window extension. Long stylistic tails are the job of `trailIntensity`, not `shutterAngle`.
Weight curves — triangle / box blended by flatness

Weights interpolate between triangle and box via `flatness = clamp((shutterAngle - 360) / 360, 0, 1)`. At `shutterAngle = 360°`, flatness is 0 and the weights are pure triangle; at `720°`, flatness is 1 and the weights are flat. Three curves are available — triangle, box, exponential — but triangle is the default, drifting naturally toward flat as `shutterAngle` grows. The final weight array is normalized by the sum, so total energy stays conserved regardless of window size.
Swift mirror — `FilmtoneMotionBlurMath`

If iOS export ran a different formula, preview and export would diverge in color. The Swift side is hand-mirrored, and `scripts/swift/test-motion-blur-math.swift` runs as part of `verify:swift-contract` to confirm boundary values (0° / 180° / 360° / 540° / 720°) match the TS output. The check is wired into `bun run --cwd apps/capacitor-film-lab-ios verify:swift-contract`.
Boundary behavior at default 8 slots

items: `0°` / `180°` — inactive, pass-through (1 frame)
`360°` — active, 2 frames, weights `[2/3, 1/3]` (triangle, flatness=0)
`540°` — active, 3 frames, weights between triangle and box at flatness ≈ 0.5
`720°` — active, 3 frames, weights `[1/3, 1/3, 1/3]` (flatness=1, fully flat)

sections.text: Aligned with industry conventions

Treating shutter angle as exposure duration matches how the rest of the industry models it. RED's Shutter Angle docs use `180° = 0.5 frame`. Foundry Nuke (Kronos and the render motion blur node) separates Shutter Time from Shutter Samples. Blender Cycles and EEVEE, plus Houdini Mantra, all expose shutter time, shutter offset, and motion samples as independent axes. Adobe AE Pixel Motion Blur generates intermediate samples from optical flow and integrates them along a shutter curve. Filmtone is a ring-buffer approximation rather than a physically accurate shutter simulator, but the meaning of `shutterAngle` is intentionally aligned with all of these.

`shutterAngle` controls only the target shutter-window extension; `trailIntensity` carries the expressive afterimage outside that window. Mixing the two blurs the meaning of `shutterAngle`, so UI copy and math both keep them apart. Want a long echo? Push `trailIntensity`. Want a different shutter feel? Move `shutterAngle`.
Splitting Source Profile and Look into two slots

Filmtone holds `.cube` LUTs in two slots. `inputLut` is source-specific: camera transforms, Apple Log to Rec.709, anything tied to the material. `creativeLut` is look-specific: the creative / stylistic LUT layered on top of a Filmtone preset. With one slot, swapping cameras either wipes the look or forces you to give up the camera transform to keep the look. Two slots let both responsibilities coexist.
Data model

The legacy `lut` field stays for decode compatibility only. Current export-request builds set `lut: nil` and transport `inputLut` and `creativeLut` independently. `FilmtonePhase0Math.buildExportRequest` enforces this, and `verify:swift-contract`'s Phase0 fixtures verify it on every gate.
Export order is fixed

items: input LUT — Source Profile / Camera transform
base grade — the Filmtone preset core (params)
tone compression
edge optics — lens softness, RGB shift
glow family — bloom, halation, diffusion
vignette
grain
creative LUT — the look's final pass
print — the last touch of paper-print character

sections.text: Input lands first (the source enters Filmtone's working space) and creative lands last (the look sits on top as the final layer). The ordering is fixed and the same in preview and export; `verify:swift-contract` keeps them in lockstep.
Replacement preserves look, not source profile

When the source is replaced (a different video, a different camera), `inputLut` is dropped — the new material likely needs a different transform. `creativeLut` is preserved because look should be independent of material. `clearInputLut()` and `clearCreativeLut()` are completely independent APIs; neither pulls the other along.
Funneling all LUT mutation through one helper

Every LUT change goes through `applyLutMutation`. It updates `updatedAt`, invalidates the rendered output state (preview task, compare frame, export result, export progress) in one shot, persists, and reschedules a preview render. Setters (`setInputLutIntensity`, `setCreativeLutIntensity`) call the same helper, so callers don't have to track the side-effect cascade themselves.
Linear intensity blending in Core Image

`FilmtoneExportSession.applyLut` returns the LUT result directly when `PreparedLut.intensity >= 0.999`. Below that, it scales alpha to `intensity` via `CIColorMatrix`, then composites the alpha-scaled LUT image over the source via `CISourceOverCompositing`. The result is `lut * intensity + original * (1 - intensity)`. The `>= 0.999` early return keeps the common 100% path off the compositing cost.
How intensity travels from UI to rendering

SwiftUI Slider → `setInputLutIntensity(value)` → `clampLutIntensity(0...1)` → `ParsedCubeLutDTO.withIntensity(clamped)` → `applyLutMutation` → `schedulePreviewRender` → preview rebuild. Export request reads the same project state, and `makePreparedLut(from: SerializableLutDTO?)` carries `PreparedLut.intensity` straight into `applyLut`. Nobody can override intensity midstream — there's no second source of truth.

Auto input transforms (Apple Log → Rec.709 etc.) are not custom LUTs and are out of scope for the intensity slider. `makeAutomaticInputLut(for:)` builds them from `request.sourceProbe?.inputTransformPolicy` along a separate path. Custom and Auto share the same `inputLut` slot mutually exclusively: when Custom is loaded, Auto is suppressed; clearing Custom with `Auto` puts the automatic transform back.
Putting TypeScript at the center

Filmtone runs preview (web / WebGL / WebGPU) and export (Desktop / iOS Swift) on separate runtimes. Keeping color identical across them depends on a single source of truth for the math. Color transforms, motion blur, exposure, LUT constraints, and preset definitions all live in TypeScript under `packages/film-lab-renderer/src/`. Swift isn't hand-written; it's generated from TS. GLSL fragment shaders and WGSL compute shaders read constants from the same TS module.
generate:filmtone-ios-swift

The root `bun run generate:filmtone-ios-swift` runs `scripts/generate-filmtone-ios-swift.ts`, which writes `apps/capacitor-film-lab-ios/ios/App/App/FilmtonePhase0Generated.swift`. It's chained into `dev:ios` and `build:ios`, so any TS change reaches the next Capacitor sync / sim build automatically.
Shape of the generated Swift module

The output is a single `enum FilmtonePhase0Generated` of static lets. `schemaVersion`, `paramKeys`, `quickAxisIds`, `defaultQuickState`, `outputProfile`, `resetParams`, and the preset definitions are copied verbatim from TS values into Swift constants. The file is marked do-not-edit; any manual change is overwritten by the next generation. Swift call-sites only read it: `FilmtonePhase0Generated.resetParams`, etc.

Motion blur math — `FilmtoneMotionBlurMath` active frames and weights at boundary values
Cube parser — `.cube` DOMAIN_MIN / DOMAIN_MAX semantics and LUT size constraints
Cache store — retention and cleanup policy
Source-color-classifier — SDR / HDR PQ / HDR HLG / Apple Log / Apple Log 2 classification and HDR preparation policy
