sections.text: Why the math doesn't drift between WebGL/WebGPU and iOS

TypeScript fans out into three downstream paths: the WebGL Backend assembles GLSL strings from TS constants under `packages/film-lab-renderer/src/webgl/`, the WebGPU Backend emits WGSL constants from `packages/film-lab-renderer/src/webgpu/`, and iOS Swift gets `FilmtonePhase0Generated.swift` from `bun run generate:filmtone-ios-swift`. All three converge on the same TypeScript functions at their entry. There is no place where someone could quietly substitute a slightly different number — the path doesn't exist.

Trying to hold color parity through discipline alone means PR reviewers spending forever spotting `Math.abs(0.18) === 0.18`-class mirror drift. Filmtone holds it through structure: TS is truth, Swift is generated, shaders import constants. If nothing is hand-mirrored, hand-mirror typos can't happen.
Capacitor 7.4 hybrid layout

Filmtone iOS is a hybrid app on top of Capacitor 7.4.3. It hosts the web shell (`packages/film-lab-ui` + React 19.2) inside a `WKWebView`, and exposes iOS-only APIs (PhotoLibrary, Core Image, AVFoundation, ActivityKit) to TypeScript through the `FilmtoneMediaPlugin` bridge. Only the things the web layer can't reach become native; UI and editor logic stay in the web side.
Eight bridge methods
What each method owns

items: `pickSource` — picks a photo or video via `PHPickerViewController`
`pickLutFile` — picks a `.cube` file via `UIDocumentPickerViewController` (accepts `{ slot?: "inputLut" | "creativeLut" }`)
`probeSource` — extracts codec, color, resolution, duration, and input-transform policy from `AVAsset`
`renderPreviewFrame` — renders one Core Image preview frame for the current project state
`runExport` — full export (mezzanine, depth, sidecar). Streams progress to TS via the `exportProgress` notify event
`saveToPhotos` — writes the output to PhotoLibrary via `PHPhotoLibrary`
`shareOutput` — presents `UIActivityViewController`
`cancelExport` — stops an in-flight export through `ExportCancelController`

sections.text: TypeScript proxy

The TS side calls `registerPlugin<FilmtoneMediaPlugin>("FilmtoneMedia", { web: ... })` and pins the contract in the interface type. The web fallback (`filmtoneMedia.web.ts`) only runs in dev when the web shell is exercised standalone. Export progress is consumed via `addListener("exportProgress", ...)`.
runExport — detached Task plus a progress stream

`runExport` decodes a `Phase0ExportRequestDTO`, builds a session via `FilmtoneMediaRuntime.makeExportSession`, then launches `runtime.runExport` inside a `Task.detached(priority: .userInitiated)`. Progress comes back through a closure and goes to TS as `notifyListeners("exportProgress", ...)`. Concurrent exports are rejected with `FilmtoneMediaError.exportBusy` if `currentExportTask` is non-nil — there's no silent fallback.
cancelExport and Live Activity share one stop point

`cancelExport` calls `ExportCancelController.shared.cancel(reason: .userViaUI)` and idempotently nudges `currentExportSession?.cancel()` and `task?.cancel()`. The Live Activity side (Lock Screen and Dynamic Island) routes through `CancelExportIntent`, which calls the same controller. UI, Lock Screen, and Dynamic Island all funnel into one cancel point with a unified reason vocabulary that ends up in the benchmark record.
Memory warning observer (not exposed to TS)

The plugin subscribes to `UIApplication.didReceiveMemoryWarningNotification` in `load()` and increments a counter from `@objc private func handleMemoryWarning()`. It's deliberately not registered as a `pluginMethod` (TS shouldn't call it). The current value lands in `Phase0ExportBenchmarkRecordDTO.memoryWarningCount` for post-export analysis.
Double-save guard for saveToPhotos

`saveToPhotos` keeps `inFlightPhotoSaveURI` and `lastSavedPhotoURI` behind an `NSLock`, rejecting concurrent saves of the same URI and any second save with `FilmtoneMediaError.saveFailed`. The app's invariant — never write the same export to Photos twice — is enforced physically at the plugin entry.

When extending the bridge, ship the TS proxy (`src/native/filmtoneMedia.ts`) and the Swift plugin (`FilmtoneMediaPlugin.swift`) in the same PR. Updating one side alone leaves a method name unresolved at runtime; preview, export, or save can fail silently. This is the most common failure mode in any project that touches a Capacitor bridge.
Splitting fastlane into six lanes by responsibility

Filmtone iOS's `fastlane/Fastfile` is split into six lanes. Each lane owns a single stage of the pipeline — build the IPA, stage review assets, submit for review — with no spillover side effects (no implicit re-archive, no surprise screenshot regeneration, no quiet metadata overwrite). The same Fastfile drives both CI and a laptop without surprises.

items: `archive` — builds the IPA at `build/fastlane/Filmtone.ipa` with Xcode automatic signing
`screenshots` — runs the UI test rail on iPhone 17 Pro Max (hard-coded UDID), then stages output for `ja` and `en-US`
`metadata` — uploads localized metadata, review info, and release notes to App Store Connect. Never touches binary or screenshots
`beta` — uploads an existing IPA to TestFlight. Always requires explicit `IPA_PATH`
`release` — uploads IPA + metadata + screenshots to ASC. `SUBMIT_FOR_REVIEW=1` submits for review; `AUTOMATIC_RELEASE=1` auto-releases on approval
`submit_review` — re-submits an already-uploaded build for review without touching binary or screenshots, given `APP_VERSION` and `BUILD_NUMBER`

sections.text: Fail-fast when no IPA is provided

`beta`, `release`, and `submit_review` all funnel through `explicit_ipa_path!(options, lane:)`. Skip `ipa:` and the lane bails immediately with `UI.user_error!`. Without this, CI quietly reuses a stale archive, or running release locally with no archive triggers a surprise 30-minute build.

def explicit_ipa_path!(options, lane:)
  explicit_path = options[:ipa] || options["ipa"]
  UI.user_error!(
    "Pass ipa:... to `fastlane ios #{lane}`. Implicit archive fallback is disabled."
  ) if explicit_path.nil?

  ipa_path = File.expand_path(explicit_path, APP_ROOT)
  UI.user_error!("IPA not found at #{ipa_path}") unless File.exist?(ipa_path)
  ipa_path
end
Trap 1 — gym 2.233 passes auth args twice

Fastlane 2.233.0's gym (`build_app`) forwards both `export_xcargs` and `xcargs` to `xcodebuild -exportArchive` during the export step. If the Fastfile sets the same App Store Connect auth args (`-authenticationKeyIssuerID` / `-authenticationKeyID` / `-authenticationKeyPath`) in both `xcargs` and `export_xcargs`, `xcodebuild -exportArchive` receives them twice and dies with `Exit status: 64`. The Xcode archive itself succeeds, only IPA export fails.
Minimum-viable fix: keep auth args in `xcargs` and don't set `export_xcargs`. Fastlane internally reuses `xcargs` during export, so the args reach `xcodebuild -exportArchive` once.

lane :archive do
  xcargs_parts = ["-allowProvisioningUpdates"]
  if asc_api_key_configured?
    key_file_path = temp_key_path || File.expand_path(env!("ASC_KEY_PATH"), APP_ROOT)
    xcargs_parts.concat([
      "-authenticationKeyIssuerID", env!("ASC_ISSUER_ID"),
      "-authenticationKeyID", env!("ASC_KEY_ID"),
      "-authenticationKeyPath", key_file_path,
    ])
  end
  xcargs = xcargs_parts.map(&:shellescape).join(" ")

  build_app(
    workspace: IOS_WORKSPACE,
    scheme: "App",
    clean: true,
    export_method: "app-store",
    output_directory: BUILD_OUTPUT_DIR,
    output_name: "Filmtone",
    build_path: BUILD_OUTPUT_DIR,
    xcargs: xcargs,
    export_options: {
      method: "app-store",
      signingStyle: "automatic",
      teamID: DEVELOPMENT_TEAM_ID,
    }
  )
end

Xcode 26.4's `xcodebuild -help` lists `app-store` as deprecated; the current name is `app-store-connect`. But fastlane 2.233.0's gym still validates against the old method names, so `export_method: "app-store"` stays. Manual `xcodebuild -exportArchive` prints a deprecation warning but still exports successfully.
Trap 2 — release_notes silently dropped means `whatsNew` is missing

Even when `fastlane/metadata/{ja,en-US}/release_notes.txt` exists on disk, calling `upload_to_app_store` without explicitly passing `release_notes:` makes the ASC API treat `whatsNew` as unset. Binary upload, screenshot upload, precheck, and build selection all succeed — then `submit_for_review: true` fails with:

appStoreVersions ... is not in valid state.
The provided entity is missing a required attribute - You must provide a value for the attribute 'whatsNew' with this request

Fix: pass `release_notes:` explicitly. The same payload is needed in `metadata`, `release`, and `submit_review`, so factor it into a helper and reference it from each lane. TestFlight (`beta` lane) wants `localized_build_info` shaped as `{ locale => { whats_new: text } }`, so a second helper re-shapes the same source.

def localized_release_note_texts
  {
    "ja" => read_text_if_present(File.join(METADATA_TEMPLATE_PATH, "ja", "release_notes.txt")),
    "en-US" => read_text_if_present(File.join(METADATA_TEMPLATE_PATH, "en-US", "release_notes.txt")),
  }.compact
end

def localized_build_release_notes
  localized_release_note_texts.each_with_object({}) do |(locale, notes), memo|
    memo[locale] = { whats_new: notes }
  end
end
submit_review — re-submit an existing build without touching the binary

When `release` failed at `submit_for_review` due to missing `whatsNew`, the binary was already at ASC. No need to re-archive — only metadata and the review submission need to land. That's exactly what `submit_review` does. It pulls `APP_VERSION` and `BUILD_NUMBER` from env or lane options, then runs `upload_to_app_store` with `skip_binary_upload: true`, `skip_screenshots: true`, `skip_metadata: false`.

lane :submit_review do |options|
  app_version = normalized_env("APP_VERSION") || options[:app_version]
  build_number = normalized_env("BUILD_NUMBER") || options[:build_number]

  UI.user_error!("Set APP_VERSION or pass app_version:") unless app_version
  UI.user_error!("Set BUILD_NUMBER or pass build_number:") unless build_number

  upload_to_app_store(
    api_key: load_asc_api_key!,
    app_identifier: APP_IDENTIFIER,
    app_version: app_version,
    build_number: build_number,
    platform: "ios",
    metadata_path: stage_metadata!,
    skip_binary_upload: true,
    skip_screenshots: true,
    skip_metadata: false,
    submit_for_review: true,
    automatic_release: truthy_env?("AUTOMATIC_RELEASE"),
    release_notes: localized_release_note_texts,
    # ...
  )
end
Closing the screenshot-asymmetry door upstream

Because `release` will overwrite ASC screenshots, mismatched per-locale counts or filenames corrupt the App Store screenshot panel. The Fastfile runs `validate_release_screenshots!` before any upload: both `ja` and `en-US` must have 1–10 screenshots, with identical filename order across locales. Anything else fails fast via `UI.user_error!`.

def validate_release_screenshots!
  screenshot_paths = staged_release_screenshot_paths
  missing_locales = screenshot_paths.select { |_, paths| paths.empty? }.keys
  unless missing_locales.empty?
    UI.user_error!("Missing staged screenshots for locales: #{missing_locales.join(', ')}")
  end

  counts = screenshot_paths.transform_values(&:count)
  unless counts.values.all? { |count| count.between?(1, 10) }
    UI.user_error!("Each locale must have between 1 and 10 screenshots.")
  end
  unless counts.values.uniq.one?
    UI.user_error!("Screenshot counts differ by locale.")
  end

  expected_basenames = nil
  screenshot_paths.each do |locale, paths|
    basenames = paths.map { |path| File.basename(path) }
    expected_basenames ||= basenames
    next if basenames == expected_basenames
    UI.user_error!("Screenshot filenames must match across locales.")
  end
end

The `release` lane only overwrites ASC screenshots when `OVERWRITE_SCREENSHOTS=1`, but for ASO-only metadata edits, prefer `metadata` or `submit_review` and don't run `release:screenshots` unless explicitly requested. The v1.1 screenshot set is the canonical state.
Count the dots

Watch the loop above and count. It starts at 6. As the lattice opens, one dot appears at the center — 7. Six more join along the outer edge — 13. An inner ring of six completes the bloom — 19. On the close the inner ring fades first, then the center and the edge together, back to 6.

All 19 dots exist from the first frame, and not a single one is ever created. Each dot just raises its `scale` on its own cue, and the cues land in order — center, then edge, then inner ring — a few frames apart. That stagger is the whole reason the count seems to grow. Which frame each dot stands up on lives in `grow`, the little key table each row of the `DOTS` blueprint carries.
The disappearing side is keyed the same way — the inner ring first, then the center and the edge together, shrinking away on the last segment of their `grow` tables.
Set up the lattice and the breath

items: 6 dots that never disappear — standing on the hexagon's vertices, the base of the lattice
1 center, 6 inner-ring and 6 edge dots — 13 waiting for their cue
edge dots stand between the vertices

sections.text: The motor is a single number that says how far the lattice has opened — it climbs from 0 (closed) to 1 (fully open), holds for a while, and falls back to 0. Which frames it opens on, where it holds, when it closes — the `BREATH` key table in the code below carries that whole split. Call it the breath.

What the breath directly drives is the hexagon's radius — the center-to-vertex distance. The breath value fills the gap between `RADIUS_REST` (closed) and `RADIUS_PEAK` (fully open) as-is. The whole lattice also rotates across the same spans, but not from the breath value — the rotation keeps its own key table and curves, the `SPIN` in the code below. To put it into code, a single part is enough: a function that fills the space between keys with a curve.
This `keyAt` is nearly the only part the article needs. A key table is just rows of “on which frame, which value, and which curve fills the next segment”.

The curves are specified with the same 4 numbers as CSS `cubic-bezier()`. The `cubicBezier` in the code below comes from `import cubicBezier from "bezier-easing"` — npm's `bezier-easing` takes the 4 numbers and returns the curve function that fills a segment. Outside its range it returns the end values, so the stillness before and after the motion costs nothing.
`DOTS` is the 19-row blueprint. Each row carries a role, an angle, a distance, and `grow` — a little key table for appearing and leaving. The 6 base dots carry no `grow` and simply stand.

The distance written in a row is used as-is only for the center and the inner ring — for the 6 base dots the breath's radius decides it, and for the 6 edge dots the `RAIL` decides it, every frame. The angles start from the hexagon's 6 vertex directions; the base and the inner ring stand on those directions, and only the edge dots stand between them.
Placement is exactly the `dotXY` in the code — walk from `CENTER` along the dot's angle by its distance and draw a circle there. The screen's y axis points down, hence the minus sign on `Math.sin`.
Drive it with `requestAnimationFrame`: compute `frame = (sec * FPS) % LOOP_FRAMES` from the elapsed seconds and you get the same loop as the demo above.

Only the six edge dots carry one more independent motion — a radius round trip that slides on its own frame ranges, separate from the breath. Both the destinations and the ranges live in the `RAIL` key table in the code above. The build started from the idea that every dot moves by one shared rule, but checking the numbers against the original video showed the edge dots alone didn't fit. Instead of forcing them under the shared rule, they keep their own keys.

Rewrite the `DOTS` table and the lattice becomes a different picture. Square up the layout and the count still seems to grow, as long as the cue stagger survives; let the breath drive opacity instead of the radius and the same skeleton wears a different face.
Why the loop seam disappears

What makes it work is the per-loop rotation amount — `SPIN_DEGREES` in the code. A hexagonal lattice returns to the same pose whenever it turns by one vertex step, and `SPIN_DEGREES` is an exact multiple of that step, so the landing is indistinguishable from the initial layout — the last frame coincides with the first and the loop seam disappears.
Overshoot, then settle

The center and the inner ring appear with character: their `grow` tables overshoot past full size, then settle back over one more segment — that is the overshoot. The edge's `grow` just rises straight to full size. The breath, too, opens and closes on separate easing curves instead of reusing a single shape. Where character rides and where the rise stays plain — that choice is what gives this motion its face.

The source is one cell of PuttiMW's (@PuttiMW) drawer series — decomposed and rebuilt in a motion-research repo. The palette swaps the reference red/pink for the fixed light palette. The texture on the demo above — grain and chromatic aberration — is composited live by the video-finishing package we are building in-house: everything from the easing solver to the grain randomness is our own code. Where `WebGPU` is unavailable it falls back to `SVG` + `requestAnimationFrame`.

sections.caption: the order is the same every loop

sections.text: Try to call the next dot

Watch the loop and try to call which dot pops next. Bottom-right goes first. Then the middle of the top row, then the middle of the bottom row — it reads as scattered, yet the order is exactly the same every loop. Bottom-left pops last, and the loop hands back to bottom-right.

What looks scattered is not a random number. The motion is a single clip, and 9 duplicates replay that same clip staggered `STEP_FRAMES` frames apart. Which duplicate starts when is decided by one fixed order table — 9 grid cells, each holding its place in line: the `ORDER` table in the code. That one table is the entire "random". The smaller the number in a cell, the earlier it moves — bottom-right leads.
Build exactly one clip

items: pop from the rest radius `R_REST` up to `R_PEAK`
drop too far, to `R_UNDER` — a key placed deliberately low
recover to `R_HOLD`, then hold it for a long stretch
one final ease back to the rest radius `R_REST`

sections.text: The clip is just 6 radius keyframes and 5 easing curves, one per segment. Put into code, it is one fill-between-keys function and 2 tables.

Each row of the `keyAt` table carries the curve that fills the next segment — the same 4 numbers as CSS `cubic-bezier()`, which npm's `bezier-easing` takes as-is. Outside its range it returns the end values — all the stillness before and after the clip comes from that alone.
A segment between equal values cannot move no matter what its curve says. That is how the long hold in `CLIP` is made — there is no dedicated hold machinery at all.

Placement is just 9 dots fixed on a 3×3 grid at a near-uniform pitch — only the radius moves. Drive it with `requestAnimationFrame`: compute `frame = (sec * FPS) % LOOP_FRAMES` from the elapsed seconds, and you get a loop the same length as the demo above.

The return after the pop lands exactly on the rest radius `R_REST`. The original video trails a faint tail that never quite returns to `R_REST` — but the last duplicate's clip starts latest and ends right at the loop's edge, using up nearly all `LOOP_FRAMES` frames. Chasing the tail would break the loop seam. So the tail was dropped, in favor of a loop whose last frame lines up exactly with its first.
Why it reads as scattered

The duplicates carry no individuality. Pop size and curve shape are shared by all dots — align all 9 on their start frames and overlay them, and the spread all but vanishes. Only the start frame differs, and for every dot that shift measures exactly `STEP_FRAMES` × the table's number. No shuffle, no random seed — the same frame always returns the same pose.
Keys, not a spring

Pop, overshoot, settle — it looks like a spring. But even the best-fit spring equation leaves a clearly measurable miss, while the 6-keyframe build shrinks the miss to a fraction of that. Even so, the deciding evidence is not how close the equations get. It sits at the exit of the hold.

Through the hold the radius barely drifts — a dead-flat stillness. Right after it, the radius velocity switches in one step from standing still to shrinking. A spring that keeps oscillating cannot produce that switch. The undershoot is not physics ringing out — it is a key someone placed.

Who moves the side squares?

While the center square makes its quarter turn, the side squares slide outward, seem to pause around the diamond, and come back. The three motions are perfectly bound together — so what is doing the binding?

Only the center's rotation carries keyframes — three of them. The sides have none. Their position is computed every frame: the closest spot that stays just clear of the spinning square. The linkage is one rotation plus a one-line contact law.
Write one rotation and one line of law

items: 3 rotation keys — upright to the diamond, then back to upright (frames and values sit in the `THETA` table)
one easing curve per segment, two in total
zero keyframes on the side squares
the push distance grows from zero to its peak, then returns to zero

sections.text: Now put it into code. The parts: one fill-between-keys function, the rotation's key table, and the one-line law — measure “half the width of the rotated square” every frame, and push each side out by however much it grew over rest. That is all.

Each row of the `keyAt` table carries the curve that fills the next segment — the same 4 numbers as CSS `cubic-bezier()`. Outside its range it returns the end values, so the upright stretch before the first key costs nothing.

`((angle % QUARTER_DEG) + QUARTER_DEG) % QUARTER_DEG` folds any angle, however many turns it has made, into one stretch from zero to `QUARTER_DEG`. That is why the width line is written as "distance from `DIAMOND_DEG`" — feed it any angle and it works.

A square of side `SIDE` is exactly `SIDE` wide while it stands upright. At the diamond its diagonal turns sideways and the width grows by a factor of `Math.SQRT2` — that growth becomes the push, which travels from zero to its peak and back to zero. Right and left move by the same formula, symmetric, with no time offset. `GAP` is the clearance that keeps them just short of touching.

To place it, set three squares of side `SIDE` at the same height and rotate only the center one by `rotate(angle)`. Drive it with `requestAnimationFrame`: compute `frame = (sec * FPS) % LOOP_FRAMES` from the elapsed seconds and you get the same loop length as the demo above.

To play with it, feed in more rotation. The law repeats every `QUARTER_DEG`, so a quarter turn yields 1 push and a half turn really does yield 2 — the count is never decided in advance; it follows from the rotation you feed in.
Why it seems to stop at the diamond

The apparent stop near the diamond is not a key holding anything. Around the diamond the width barely changes, so the push barely changes — a fake stop created by the shape itself. Measured, the rotation's speed through the diamond is small but not zero. The rotation never stops.
Is it really touching?

From the push trajectory alone you can solve backwards: if the sides really are touching, what must the square's side length be? The recovered side matches the side measured independently from the video. The remaining gap also stays nearly constant across the whole travel. A size that matches and a gap that holds still — those two are contact's fingerprints.

You could also key the sides by hand — 13 keys fit slightly better. That explanation was still thrown out: if the sides were keyed by hand, the side length recovered from their track matching the real square would be pure coincidence. The apparent left–right offset also vanished under finer measurement — false evidence manufactured by a coarse measuring method.

sections.caption: they trade sizes, the kiss point never moves

sections.text: Stare at the kiss point

In the loop above, the bottom-right circle inflates by exactly as much as the top-left circle deflates, and over the first half of the loop they trade sizes; the second half trades them back. Now stare at the single point where the two circles touch — however far the trade goes, that contact point never moves once in the whole loop.

This motion is named "inverse proportion" — the textbook relation where one quantity grows as the other shrinks. In a true inverse proportion, multiplying the two radii (their product) would give the same number on every frame. Measure the original, though, and it does not. What stays constant is the addition instead: the two radii always add up to the value `R_SUM` holds in the code. Keyframes sit only on the top-left circle's radius — 3 of them. The bottom-right radius is "`R_SUM` minus the top-left", and carries not a single key.
Write one radius and a one-line subtraction

items: 3 radius keys — `R_REST` at both ends, `R_MID` at the turnaround
one easing curve per segment, two in total
bottom-right radius: zero keys — just `R_SUM` minus the top-left
both centres: zero keys — each recedes from the fixed contact point by its own radius

sections.text: The placement of the centres is the heart of the build. Fix a single contact point on the diagonal; each circle puts its centre its own radius away from that point — the top-left circle up-left along the axis, the bottom-right circle down-right. That goes into code as-is. The only machinery it needs is a single fill-between-keys function.

Each row of the `keyAt` table carries the curve that fills the next segment — the same 4 numbers as CSS `cubic-bezier()`. The shrink and the grow are similar but separate, 1 each — reuse one of them for both, and the error against the measurement grows several times over.

As the radii change the centres slide on their own, and the circles kiss at that point on every frame — no key ever aligns the contact. The point held still in the opening because it is built to hold still. Drive it with `requestAnimationFrame`: compute `frame = (sec * FPS) % LOOP_FRAMES` from the elapsed seconds, and you get a loop the same length as this demo.

To play with it, add keys. Grow the radius keys from 3 to 5 — `R_REST`→`R_MID`→`R_REST`→`R_MID`→`R_REST` — and the same function fits 2 round-trips of the trade into one loop. Change `R_SUM` and the pair's total changes with it — the one-line subtraction never breaks.
The crossing moment picked the equation

The product and sum equations part ways at the moment the circles pass at equal size. The crossing comes partway through the shrink, with both radii at exactly half of `R_SUM`. Keep a product unchanged while pushing two numbers closer together, and their sum always shrinks. So if the product were constant, the radius sum would have to sag clearly toward this moment. The measured sum barely changes between rest and the crossing — no sag anywhere. Next to the constant-sum fit, the product model's miss is larger by an order of magnitude — so it was thrown out.
No key parks the bottom

At the bottom of the shrink, the motion seems to rest for a while. The first measurement agreed: "there is a hold key here". But that was a fake stillness, created by a habit of the measuring program — it recycled the previous frame's answer as the starting point for the next one. Break the habit, measure again, and the stillness dissolves into a single very shallow valley.

The settled build has no hold key. The motion seems to rest because the tail of the one curve each segment owns is long and gentle, easing slowly toward its target value. The tail also carries a small expression — it slips just past the target before settling back, so the radius bottoms just shy of `MID_FRAME` rather than on it, and peaks just shy of the loop seam. The valley and the peak measured independently from the original point to nearly the same spots.

sections.caption: the tail is 9 replays of the past

sections.text: Count the tail

2 dots make one full lap around a circle and stop. Watch the tail on the way — in the fast stretch it splits apart, one copy at a time, like a flip-book. In the slow stretch it melts into a continuous band. The moment they stop, the tail is gone — just 2 dots again.

Only one thing is animated: a single rotation. Every layer of the tail is a copy replaying that same rotation slightly late — copy 1 runs `DELAY_FRAMES` behind, copy 2 twice that, and so on through 9 copies. Opacity thins by a factor of `DECAY` per copy. The afterimage is the dot's own past, replayed.
Set up one rotation and 9 copies

items: dot radius `DOT_RADIUS` — 2 of them, on exactly opposite sides of the center
orbit radius `ORBIT_RADIUS`
2 rotation keys — the rest angle at the start, exactly one full lap by frame `SWEEP_FRAMES`, one easing curve
frames `SWEEP_FRAMES` to `LOOP_FRAMES`: rest, no rotation keys there
9 copies — each one `DELAY_FRAMES` further into the past, each `DECAY`× the opacity

sections.text: That's every part. Assembly is one function: pass a frame number, get back the list of circles to draw — compute 1 rotation, and let the copies read it shifted into the past.
`ease` holds the entire face of this motion. It is exactly the math of CSS `cubic-bezier()` — npm's `bezier-easing` takes the 4 numbers passed to `ease` as-is.
The curve's shape: a deep slow start, a speed peak near the middle of the sweep, then a long soft landing. Change the 4 numbers and only the pacing changes — the tail logic stays.

To put it on screen, turn each angle into a point on the orbit — center `CENTER` for both x and y, radius `ORBIT_RADIUS`: `x = CENTER + ORBIT_RADIUS * Math.cos(rad(angle))`, `y = CENTER + ORBIT_RADIUS * Math.sin(rad(angle))`. `rad()` is the one-liner that converts degrees to radians.

Then drive it with `requestAnimationFrame`: compute `frame = (sec * FPS) % LOOP_FRAMES` from elapsed seconds for the frame number — the same loop length as the demo above. `SVG` `circle` or `canvas`, either works.

The best part of this build: rotation doesn't have to be the star. Swap the `angle` line for a horizontal slide or a `scale` pulse, and the structure — stacked copies each reading slightly into the past — keeps working. Any looping motion grows a tail by the same logic.
Why the tail changes its look

The copies decide nothing — each reads the same curve, shifted into the past by its own delay. The spacing between neighboring copies is exactly how far the dot moves in `DELAY_FRAMES`. In the fastest stretch that spacing beats the dot's own width (a full diameter), so the copies pull apart and read one by one; in the slow stretches they overlap and melt into a band. Flip-book or melt is decided by speed alone.
The first measurement said half a turn

When this motion was first measured, the rotation read as half a turn per lap. The tracker followed the center of the whole smeared blob, which drags the reading backward — and with the 2 dots sitting exactly opposite each other, a half-turn error produces the same picture, so nothing flagged it.

One contradiction broke that reading. Assume half a turn, and in the fastest stretch the dense tail would sit well ahead of the dot it belongs to — no rig puts the tail in front of the dot. Re-tracking only the densest leading edge reads a full turn per lap, and the conclusion flipped. The end rest is pinned by the same measurement — nudge the last rotation key off `SWEEP_FRAMES` and the fit across all frames gets visibly worse.

Where `WebGPU` is unavailable it falls back to `SVG` + `requestAnimationFrame`.
Open, hold, return

4 tall bars stretch while splitting to the left and right. The small square in the middle swells at the same time. At full stretch, all 5 freeze for a beat — then walk the road back exactly the way they came. The left half mirrors the right, and no shape starts early or arrives late.

There are no per-shape keyframes. The only thing animated is a single number that climbs from 0 to 1, sits at 1 for a short beat, and comes back to 0 — call it the pulse. Each shape just reads that same pulse, multiplied by its own motion amount (how many px one pulse moves it), and the mirror is nothing more than the travel sign flipping between left and right. The center square even makes a half turn on the same pulse.
Set up one pulse and 5 shapes

items: 4 tall bars — width from the table's `w`, round caps, resting height from `h`
a rounded square in the middle — resting size from its `w` and `h` row, corner radius `SQUARE_CORNER`
2 outer bars: heights grow by `growH` and slide outward by `slide` — the 2 outer rows carry the larger values
2 inner bars: the same `growH` and `slide` columns, with smaller values than the outer pair
the center square: `growW` and `growH` swell both sides, `spin` gives the half turn
4 pulse keys — running 0 → 1 → (stays 1) → 0, frame positions as listed in `pulseKeys`

sections.text: That's every part. Assembly is one function: pass a frame number, get back where each shape goes — compute the pulse once, and let the 5 shapes read it through their own motion amounts.
`ease` holds the entire face of this motion. It is exactly the math of CSS `cubic-bezier()`, and npm's `bezier-easing` takes the 4 numbers written in the code as-is.

The curve starts deep and slow, rushes through the middle, and lands on a long soft tail. The way out — the first span of `pulseKeys` — is this one curve. The way back — the last span — is the same curve again: the key values run from 1 down to 0, so the same progression simply runs downhill in value. That's why going and returning wear the same face.

In between, the middle 2 keys both read 1, and the value stays put across that span. That held pause is the showpiece of this motion: change the 4 numbers of `ease` and only the pacing changes, while the key table keeps guarding the pause.

To put it on screen, make the `viewBox` a square of side `VIEWBOX` and hand the values to a `rect` — the top-left corner sits half a size away from the center (`x = cx - width / 2`), the bars' round caps come from a corner radius `rx` of `BAR_CAP`, the square's from `SQUARE_CORNER`. Rotation in SVG is 1 line, `transform="rotate(angle cx cy)"` — the shape spins about its own center.

Then drive it with `requestAnimationFrame`: compute `frame = (sec * FPS) % LOOP_FRAMES` from the elapsed seconds and you get the same loop length as the demo above. The pulse lands back on 0 at its last key and stays there across the loop edge — the seam hides inside the resting stretch.

The motion-amount table is the playground. Grow the row to 6 bars, give every `slide` the same sign so the whole row drifts one way, hand `spin` to the outer bars — the one-pulse structure keeps working. Point the pulse at opacity or color intensity instead, and the logic still holds. Wiring everything you want moving together to the same single number is the heart of this build.
Why they land in lockstep

They look coordinated not because something coordinates them, but because there is nothing that could drift: every shape reads the same single number, so the timing cannot disagree. No shape starts late — measuring the original video found no timing gap beyond measurement noise. No code knows about left versus right either; all that exists is the ± sign on the travel. Even the freeze at full stretch is no special case — it is just the span where the keys run from 1 to 1, made visible.
The rotation vanished from the first measurement

The first measurement of this motion concluded that the center square does not rotate. The square is the smallest of the 5, and a check that compares how silhouettes overlap barely notices which way a small shape points — compare only the moments where the square looks upright (its unrotated orientation), and the pose after a half turn makes the exact same picture as no turn at all.

The crack showed up in the size reading. On frames where rotation mixes in, only the box drawn around the shape swells — while the painted area doesn't grow at all. A box that fattens with no extra area is the proof that the shape inside is tilted.

Re-reading the angle from the shape's proportions: the square makes a half turn per pulse — `spin` in the code is that value. A quarter-turn theory predicts a clearly tilted diamond at a moment on the way out — the observation there is upright. A full-turn theory predicts a return to upright partway through — the observation there is a diamond. Only the half turn fits every place a diamond or an upright pose shows up.

sections.caption: One number drives the ∞ track and its dot — a loop that closes after one lap

sections.text: Sprint, crawl, sprint again

A thick stroke and the dot riding its head keep tracing an ∞-shaped track. Most of the lap goes by in one whip-like burst; only one remaining stretch crawls. It reads like a two-gear lap — but there is no gear mechanism anywhere.

You choose only 2 speed keys — one whip's worth. The third key's value follows automatically from the promise that `PERIOD_FRAMES` frames close exactly 1 lap — nobody decided the crawl's speed. The line never stretches either: a fixed-length window covering `DRAWN_FRACTION` of the full path slides along the track.
Set up a track, a window and a dot

items: A closed ∞-shaped track — this demo runs the idealized one with perfectly round lobes, the original is a slightly distorted ∞ drawn with 4 pen-tool anchors
A thick stroke (`STROKE_WIDTH` px wide on a `VIEWBOX` px-square canvas) covering `DRAWN_FRACTION` of the track's length taken as 1 — the undrawn `GAP_FRACTION` becomes the gap
A dot riding the head (radius `DOT_RADIUS` px) — the gap straddles the dot, front and back

The head's progress u (0 = start, 1 = a full lap) — 2 keys, the whip starts from `U_AT_WHIP_START` on frame `WHIP_START_FRAME` of the loop and covers `WHIP_SPAN` of the lap in `WHIP_DUR_FRAMES` frames

sections.text: You build 2 things: a function that turns a frame number into the head's progress u, and a way to put u on screen. The function first.

`whip` is exactly the same math as CSS `cubic-bezier()`, and npm's `bezier-easing` takes `whip`'s 4 numbers as-is. It holds back at the start, surges through the middle, then sheds speed to hand off into the crawl.

The heart is the third key's value, `U_AT_WHIP_START + 1`. The moment you decide that `PERIOD_FRAMES` frames close 1 lap, the last span can only be written as the remaining `CRAWL_SPAN` over the remaining `CRAWL_DUR_FRAMES` frames. There is no dial for the crawl's speed — to change it, grow or shrink the `WHIP_SPAN` the whip eats. Change the leftover and the crawl changes on its own.

Two conversions put it on screen. For the line, give the `path` a `pathLength={1}` so the track's length reads as 1, then set `stroke-dasharray` to `DRAWN_FRACTION GAP_FRACTION` and `stroke-dashoffset` to `DRAWN_FRACTION + PAINT_HEAD_LAG - u`. The window slides, pulled by u, and the gap shifts by `PAINT_HEAD_LAG` to straddle the dot.
The dot's coordinates come from `getPointAtLength(u × total length)`. The browser already turns distance along a path into a point — you only write up to u.

Drive it with `requestAnimationFrame`: compute `frame = (sec * FPS) % PERIOD_FRAMES` from the elapsed seconds and that is the frame number. The loop's seam sits near the end of the crawl, and the speed across the seam is the crawl's own speed, so nothing pops at the boundary.

The track doesn't have to be an ∞. u only says how far along the track you are, so any closed path — a circle, a heart — works with the same `uKeys`. Shrink the window's `DRAWN_FRACTION` and the look turns into a half-drawn line racing the track.
Why it reads as a gear shift

The speed is designed in 1 place — the whip — and the crawl is the leftover, what the promise of a closed lap left behind. Measure the crawl in the original video and its speed is a straight line down to measurement rounding — a smoothness hand-placed keys almost never produce.
The crawl's speed fell out of arithmetic

This reproduction started as plain copying — replaying the head's position for all `PERIOD_FRAMES` frames — and it couldn't say why that speed. The rebuild started with the track: a symmetric path drawn with 4 pen-tool anchors fit better than 2 textbook ∞ formulas. The round-lobe ∞ in the demo above is the closest formula, the one that narrowly lost. We chose it for reading, knowing it is not the original's track — u's table is untouched.

Then the speed. Constant speed missed, the stock easing presets missed, and a free 3-key curve matches the numbers only by letting the speed jump several-fold at a key — a setting no human hand places. What remained was 1 whip plus the automatic straight line — and that pair predicts the crawl's speed: `CRAWL_SPAN` divided by `CRAWL_DUR_FRAMES`. The measurement agreed to within a fraction of a percent.

Where `WebGPU` is unavailable, the demo falls back to plain `SVG` + `requestAnimationFrame` rendering.
What we tried to make

The feeling of a single stroke that gets relayed across spaces — not as duplicated animations, but as multiple layers referencing one Theatre.js timeline. The same gesture, picked up by other layers with different eases, produces the relay.
The technical key

items: One Theatre.js keyframe playback as the master
Each relay layer reads the same timeline time with its own offset and ease
The phase difference between layers is what reads as 'the relay'

sections.text: What we cut

Early versions wrote a separate animation for each layer. The relay never appeared — the layers just looked unrelated. Same vocabulary across layers is the whole point, and a shared timeline is what guarantees it.
Where it could land
Hero stroke transitions, line elements during section changes. Whether it actually ships in the body is a separate decision; here it lives as documented vocabulary.
What we tried to make

Three headline lines on the same ease arrive together. Three lines on three different eases lose meaning. The aim is for the final line to carry a payoff — a small but distinct landing — without making the others noisy.
Vocabulary

items: family — share a common ease across the group
stage — assign positions (early / mid / late) within the family
payoff — give the final stage a different ease (light overshoot, soft residue)

sections.text: What we cut
Giving each line a slightly different ease was abandoned — too much information, no readable weight. The harder constraint was 'never use more than three stages.' That kept the payoff legible.
Where it could land
Hero title stagger, Filmtone step reveals, photography caption sequencing. Anywhere the same ease stretches across multiple beats.
What we tried to make

A poster reveal that opens the way paper bleeds through paper. CSS clip-path delivers only hard edges; a paper-like 'boil' isn't reachable. WebGL holds a boil field — a low-frequency noise field running on its own time — and the aperture's edge is displaced by it.
Structure

items: boil field — low-frequency noise plus a time phase, the 'simmering' surface
alpha-mask-gate — the reveal progress (0..1) for the poster
edge displacement — only the gate's rim is perturbed by the boil field

sections.text: What we cut

Pushing the boil amplitude high made the surface look like jelly, not paper. We confined the displacement to the rim and forbade modulating the interior. The moment the inside wobbles, the paper character is gone.
Where it could land
First-time poster-style reveals, Filmtone sample swaps, journal cover transitions.
What we tried to make

Carry the residue of motion past the moment it ends. The previous frames don't disappear instantly; they decay, and if new motion enters before the decay is over, the residue interferes with it. The screen is still — but something hasn't finished moving.
Structure

items: echo family — a buffer of N frames captured after the primary motion ends
decay — each captured frame loses energy exponentially over time
residue — if new motion arrives before decay completes, the remaining residue is added back into it

sections.text: What we cut

Visualizing echoes as ghost trails was abandoned. Visible ghosts read as VFX and pull the page out of the editorial register. The echo is kept numerically but contributes only a thin 5–10% of opacity to the shader output.
Where it could land
Section transitions, the trailing edge of scrolljack, the response after a Filmtone slider release. Not as VFX — as an underlayer that supports the feel of input.
